title: Linear search
starter: You have lost a photo in an album of 200 pictures. Describe exactly how you would look for it, and how many you would expect to check.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: How it works
facts: Start at the first item and compare it to what you are looking for.
If it doesn't match, move to the next and compare again.
Stop when it matches, or when you reach the end without finding it.
stations.challenge: Describe a linear search in three steps of your own.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Start at the first item and compare it to what you are looking for.
Also credit: If it doesn't match, move to the next and compare again.

questions.q: Step through a linear search for 31. Tap each item the algorithm checks, in order.
Where does a linear search start?
questions.a: At the first item in the list

stations.name: Its one great advantage
facts: The list does not need to be in order.
It works on any data that can be compared, including text.
It is short and easy to program, so mistakes are less likely.
stations.challenge: Give two situations where a linear search is the right choice.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The list does not need to be in order.
Also credit: It works on any data that can be compared, including text.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a linear search?
questions.a: It works on a list that is not in order

questions.q: Which of these suit a linear search? Select all that apply.
questions.a: A short list of names in no particular order; A list that changes every few seconds; Searching once through unsorted data; A list of only a dozen items

stations.name: Counting the checks
facts: Best case: the item is first, so one check.
Worst case: the item is last or missing, so one check per item.
On average, about half the list is checked.
stations.challenge: For a list of 100 items, state the best, worst and average number of checks.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Best case: the item is first, so one check.
Also credit: Worst case: the item is last or missing, so one check per item.

questions.q: A list has 500 items. What is the worst case for a linear search?
Step through a linear search for 5, the last item. Count how many checks it takes.

stations.name: Why it gets slow
facts: Double the list and you double the work.
For a million items, the worst case is a million comparisons.
This is why large systems sort their data and use a faster search instead.
stations.challenge: Explain why a linear search becomes unusable on very large data.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Double the list and you double the work.
Also credit: For a million items, the worst case is a million comparisons.

questions.q: A list grows from 1,000 to 2,000 items. What happens to the worst case?
Why do large systems sort their data?
questions.a: So they can use a much faster search that needs the list in order

stations.name: Writing it down
facts: Set a flag to false, then loop through every index.
If the item at that index matches, set the flag to true and stop.
After the loop, the flag says whether it was found.
stations.challenge: Write pseudocode for a linear search that outputs true or false.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Set a flag to false, then loop through every index.
Also credit: If the item at that index matches, set the flag to true and stop.

questions.q: Put these lines into a working linear search.
questions.a: found = false → for i = 0 to length(list) - 1 →   if list[i] == target then →     found = true →   endif → next i → print(found)

questions.q: Why is the flag set to false before the loop?
questions.a: So that a list with no match still gives a sensible answer

stations.name: Answering search questions
facts: Name the algorithm and say what it does step by step.
Say whether the list must be in order: for a linear search, it need not be.
If asked to count checks, count comparisons, not loops.
stations.challenge: Plan a four-mark answer describing a linear search.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Name the algorithm and say what it does step by step.
Also credit: Say whether the list must be in order: for a linear search, it need not be.

questions.q: Which is the strongest description of a linear search?
questions.a: It compares the target with each item in turn from the start, stopping when it matches or the list ends

questions.q: A question asks how many items a linear search checks to find the fifth of eight items. What is the answer?

final.name: Final challenge: search it

questions.q: Find 42 with a linear search. Tap each item the algorithm checks.
Would a linear search be a sensible choice here?
questions.a: Twelve names in no particular order = Sensible; A shopping list on your phone = Sensible; A list that is rebuilt every second = Sensible; Ten million sorted customer records = Not sensible; A dictionary searched thousands of times a second = Not sensible; Every web page on the internet = Not sensible

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe how a linear search works.
points: Say whether the list must be in order: for a linear search, it need not be.
It works on any data that can be compared, including text.
This is why large systems sort their data and use a faster search instead.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: State one advantage of a linear search over a binary search.
points: Say whether the list must be in order: for a linear search, it need not be.
This is why large systems sort their data and use a faster search instead.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

exam.q: A list contains 2,000 unsorted items. Explain why a linear search may take a long time, and state the maximum number of comparisons needed.
points: For a million items, the worst case is a million comparisons.
Say whether the list must be in order: for a linear search, it need not be.
This is why large systems sort their data and use a faster search instead.
If asked to count checks, count comparisons, not loops.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
